extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, clinical investigators, and researchers/policymakers studying peer review outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of factors that influence NIH CSR peer-review outcomes for R01 grant applications, comparing clinical (human-subjects) versus non-clinical applications and identifying measurable contributors to score differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority score (1.0–5.0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications reviewed by NIH receive a priority score, which reflects a scientific review group’s evaluation of the scientific and technical merit of the application. Individual members vote scores from 1.0 (highest merit) to 5.0 (lowest merit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores are given in 0.1 increments by individual reviewers; study sections vary in scoring behavior so priority scores are the primary within-section metric but require normalization for cross-section comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile rank (cross-study-section comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: R01 applications within each CSR study section are assigned a percentile rank according to priority scores given in the current and previous two review rounds; lower percentile = greater relative merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percentile ranks are used to provide cross-study section and longitudinal comparisons. Applications that do not receive a priority score (triaged) are still included within a study section’s percentile rankings for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage / non-competitive (no priority score)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application is deemed to be 'non-competitive' (in the lower half, qualitatively, of applications reviewed by the study section) by unanimous agreement, it will not be fully discussed at the study section meeting and will not receive a priority score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triaged applications are not discussed and receive no priority score; however, they are still incorporated into percentile rankings. The triage decision substantially affects whether an application is scored and thus its funding prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human subject concerns (human subjects protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH defines human subject concerns as any potential or actual unacceptable risk(s) or inadequate protection against risk(s) to human subjects identified in any portion of the application. Study section members are advised to factor human subject concerns in their assignment of a priority score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified human subject concerns are associated with worse peer-review outcomes: in the dataset, 14.8% of clinical R01s had human subject concerns and only ~10% of those scored within the 20th percentile vs ~19% without concerns. Thus failure to address human subject protection adequately can materially lower priority/percentile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/identification of clinical research (PI checkbox)
rubrics_metrics.description: A research application is defined as clinical when the principal investigator indicates involvement of human subjects by checking 'yes' on page 1 of the grant application form in response to the involvement of human subjects query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inclusive operational definition captures clinical trials, therapeutic interventions, outcomes, epidemiology, behavioral studies, health services research, and technology development; it excludes research using publicly available or existing deidentified data/specimens (NIH Exemption 4). Correctly identifying human-subjects involvement triggers human-subjects review expectations and codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy/completeness of the human subjects protection section
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must adequately document protections for human subjects in the designated section; inadequate explanation may lead reviewers to note human subject concerns even if the science is meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide complete information about plans to protect human subjects may result in a less favorable priority score and reduce likelihood of funding. The paper recommends improved training for investigators and potential clarification of application instructions for this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator status: new vs experienced
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction based on whether an individual has served as PI on a Public Health Service-supported research project; 'new' investigators may have been PIs on small grants (R03), R15, R21, or certain mentored K awards but not larger PHS-supported projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New investigators submitted a larger proportion of clinical A0 applications and had higher rates of human subject concerns (e.g., 19.2% for new/T1 A0). Type 1 applications from new investigators scored worse than Type 1 from established investigators; resubmissions narrowed differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application type: Type 1 (new) vs Type 2 (competing renewal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type 1 = new application; Type 2 = competing renewal/continuation application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type 1 applications generally scored worse than Type 2 applications. Clinical investigators were less likely to submit Type 2 applications, and the lower rate of competing renewal submissions by clinical investigators accounts for approximately half of the aggregate difference in peer-review outcomes between clinical and non-clinical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission/resubmission status: A0 (initial), A1, A2 (revisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are tracked as initial submissions (A0) and subsequent resubmissions (A1, A2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in clinical vs non-clinical outcomes were larger at A0 and narrowed with A1 and disappeared by A2. New investigator A0 submissions had the highest percent of human subject concerns; resubmissions tended to reduce the percent with human subject concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section assignment and reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of an application to a study section and the professional background/experience conducting clinical research among reviewers are considered potential influences on review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior analysis reported that assignment of priority scores for clinical and non-clinical applications did not differ for reviewers with or without experience conducting clinical research. Nevertheless, study section composition and appropriate assignment remain monitored and relevant to fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of clinical applications in a study section
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion ('density') of clinical applications reviewed by a study section might influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors report that differences in peer review outcomes were not accounted for by the density of clinical applications in a study section in prior analyses, but density was considered as a possible explanatory variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requested costs / budget size
rubrics_metrics.description: Total requested costs for an application (budget) were considered as a factor that might influence review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis found that greater requested costs for clinical research did not account for the less favorable review outcomes observed for clinical applications in prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory complexity / ethical/legal environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The increasing complexity of federal regulations dealing with ethical conduct of clinical research poses challenges for clinical investigators in documenting protections and may contribute to reviewer-identified concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex regulations and rise of litigation in human subjects research are potential causes of documentation problems; these systemic factors may indirectly lower peer-review outcomes for clinical applications and suggest need for institutional training and clearer instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate composition effects (proportions of subsets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall aggregate differences in percent scoring within the 20th percentile are influenced by (1) the percent of applications in each subset (e.g., Type1 vs Type2, A0 vs A1/A2) that score within the 20th percentile and (2) the proportion of each subset relative to the total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling showed that both failure to address human subjects protections and lower rates of Type 2 competing renewal submissions by clinical investigators each account for approximately half of the observed aggregate difference in outcomes between clinical and non-clinical R01 applications.
